blocks.text: A sequence \(\{a_{n}\}\) is an arithmetic sequence or arithmetic progression (A.P.) if \(a_{n} - a_{n-1}\) is the same number for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(n > 1\). The difference \(a_{n} - a_{n-1}\) \((n > 1)\), i.e. the difference of two consecutive terms of an A.P., is called the common difference and is usually denoted by \(d\).

Thus, an arithmetic progression is a sequence in which each term after the first is found by adding a constant to the previous term. This constant is called the common difference of the arithmetic progression.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: If \(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{n}, \ldots\) are in A.P., then \(d = a_{2} - a_{1} = a_{3} - a_{2} = \ldots\), where \(a_{n}\) is the \(n\)th term of the A.P.
For example: the following sequences are A.P.s.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to find \(d\): subtract any term from the term just after it (later minus earlier, never the other way).
(i) \(3 - 1 = 2\), \(5 - 3 = 2\), \(7 - 5 = 2\): constant, so A.P. with \(d = 2\).
(ii) \(51 - 54 = -3\), \(48 - 51 = -3\): constant, so A.P. with \(d = -3\). A negative \(d\) means the terms decrease.
To test whether a sequence is an A.P., check that this difference is the same all the way along; if one difference is different, it is not an A.P. For example \(2, 4, 8, \ldots\) has differences \(2, 4\), so it is not an A.P.

The \(n\)th term of an arithmetic progression can be written as:

blocks.text_alt: a sub n equals a sub 1 plus (n minus 1) times d

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why \((n - 1)d\) and not \(nd\)? Count the steps. To go from \(a_{1}\) to \(a_{2}\) we add \(d\) once; to \(a_{3}\), twice; to \(a_{n}\), \(n - 1\) times. Like the floors of a building: from the 1st floor to the 5th floor you climb only 4 staircases.
The formula links four quantities, \(a_{n}\), \(a_{1}\), \(n\) and \(d\). If any three are known, the fourth can be found. Most A.P. questions are exactly this.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
(i) The 1st, 2nd, 3rd and \(n\)th terms of an A.P. are denoted by \(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) and \(a_{n}\) respectively.
(ii) The \(n\)th term from the end of an A.P. is the \((m - n + 1)\)th term, where \(m\) denotes the total number of terms of the A.P.
(iii) Three numbers \(a, b, c\) are in A.P. if and only if \(2b = a + c\).
(iv) Any term (except the first and last) in an A.P. is equal to half of the sum of two terms equidistant from it.
(v) If the term \(a_{1}\) is unknown or not given, the \(n\)th term can be written as \(a_{n} = a_{m} + (n - m)d\) (the subscript of the given term and the coefficient of \(d\) sum to \(n\)).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Understanding the five Note points with the A.P. \(3, 7, 11, \ldots, 39\) (\(d = 4\), \(m = 10\) terms):
(ii) The 3rd term from the end is the \((10 - 3 + 1) = 8\)th term from the start, \(a_{8} = 3 + 7(4) = 31\). Counting back from the end: \(39, 35, 31\). Correct.
(iii) \(a, b, c\) in A.P. means \(b - a = c - b\), so \(2b = a + c\): the middle number is the average of the other two. Example: \(7\) is between \(3\) and \(11\), and \(2(7) = 3 + 11\).
(iv) The 5th term is 19; the terms 2 places on either side are \(a_{3} = 11\) and \(a_{7} = 27\), and \(\frac{11 + 27}{2} = 19\).
(v) Starting from a known term \(a_{m}\) instead of \(a_{1}\): \(a_{10} = a_{4} + (10 - 4)d = 15 + 6(4) = 39\). The subscript 4 and the coefficient 6 add up to 10.
The middle term of an A.P. depends upon the number of terms, e.g.,

If the total number of terms of an A.P. is even, there are two middle terms, the \(\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)\)th and the \(\left(\frac{n}{2} + 1\right)\)th, where \(n\) is the number of terms. In example (i), 5 and 7 are the two middle terms.
If the total number of terms of an A.P. is odd, there is only one middle term, the \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)\)th term. In example (ii), 7 is the only middle term.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why these positions? For \(n = 6\): positions \(1, 2, \mathbf{3}, \mathbf{4}, 5, 6\); there is no single centre, so the 3rd \(\left(\frac{6}{2}\right)\) and 4th \(\left(\frac{6}{2} + 1\right)\) terms share it: \(a_{3} = 5\), \(a_{4} = 7\).
For \(n = 7\): positions \(1, 2, 3, \mathbf{4}, 5, 6, 7\); three terms lie on each side of the 4th \(\left(\frac{7+1}{2}\right)\) term, \(a_{4} = 7\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A.P.: the difference of consecutive terms is constant; this constant is the common difference \(d = a_{n} - a_{n-1}\).
2. \(n\)th term: \(a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\).
3. \(a, b, c\) are in A.P. if and only if \(2b = a + c\).
4. \(n\)th term from the end = \((m - n + 1)\)th term from the start (\(m\) terms in all).
5. Without \(a_{1}\): \(a_{n} = a_{m} + (n - m)d\).
6. Middle term(s): the \(\frac{n}{2}\)th and \(\left(\frac{n}{2} + 1\right)\)th for even \(n\); the \(\frac{n+1}{2}\)th for odd \(n\).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Using \(a_{n} = a_{1} + nd\): the number of steps is \(n - 1\).
2. Subtracting the wrong way: \(d = a_{2} - a_{1}\) (later minus earlier); for \(54, 51, 48\), \(d = -3\), not 3.
3. Checking only the first difference: all consecutive differences must be equal.
4. Confusing the term's position with its value when finding middle terms: the middle "term" is the value in the middle position.
